chunks.text: But have we got our submitter, Mr Donaldson? Just need him to accept the approach to start.

Mr Donaldson. Kia ora. Right. Thank you. I'm Greg O'Connor, I'm the chair of the committee. Just to introduce ourselves, to my right, I have the- Kia ora, Brian. I'm Greg Fleming, national MP for Maungakiekie-Tamaki- And to my left, I have... Kia ora. I'm Celia Wade-Brown from the Greens.

Hello. Sam Athfield, Member of Parliament for Tauranga. All right. Now, Mr Donaldson, thank you for coming in and giving us your time. So now we've got 10 minutes. You can take your submission as having been read, and hopefully you'll obviously prepare to summarize that. I can see you've got your paper there, and leave time for questions at the end.

Sure thing. The airwaves are yours. Kia ora koutou. My name is Byron. I am the caregiver of my father. I have a lifelong disability. I've spent years navigating MSD and NASC and the wider disability system. I'm also speaking for the many disabled people and families who deal with the same issues but don't have the energy, confidence or support to stand here today.

My petition is simple. Remove support living payment reviews for people with lifelong disabilities. A lifelong disability does not change, but the review process keeps treating people as if it is might. Number one, the core problem. The Supported Living Payment process is unnecessary, harmful, and insignificant for people with permanent disabilities.

There are people who already have medically certified as having conditions that will not improve. They already are assessed by NASC. They are already recognized as permanently disabled by the health system. Yet MSD continues to require periodic reviews, sometimes every year, sometimes every two years, to check whether their lifelong disability is still lifelong.

This makes no sense medically, practically, or ethically. The review process creates four major harms. Number one, stress and fear. Disabled people and their families live with constant anxiety that a review could disrupt or remove essential income. Even when the review is routine, the fear is real, and for many people, the Support Living Payment is the difference between stability and crisis. Number two, administration burden.

People with lifelong disabilities often rely on carers, advocates, or overstretched support workers to manage paperwork. Reviews add unnecessary workload to people who already struggle with fatigue, cognitive load, or health struggles. Number three, system ineffectuality. MSD staff spend time processing reviews that will never result in a change. That time could be spent supporting people whose circumstances do change.

Number four, contradictions between agencies. NASC assessments already confirm permanent disability. Medical specialists already confirm permanent disability. MSD reviews ignore these certifications and require people to reprove what has already been proven.

This is not a small inconvenience. It is a structural flaw that causes real harm. Number two, real-world impacts. I want to speak to the lived reality behind this petition. My disability is lifelong. It will not improve, it will not change. Yet every review cycle, we go through the same process, gathering documents, contacting doctors, waiting for MSD responses, and hoping nothing gets lost or misinterpreted. For me, the stress is overwhelming, and as a caregiver, it is exhausting.

We are not alone. I've spoken with families who dread the envelope arriving in the mail, people who panic when MSD calls, people who have been traumatized by past interactions with government agencies and now have to relive that stress every review cycle.

Some disabled people don't have advocates, some don't have family. Some don't have the capacity to navigate bureaucracy. A review that should be simple becomes a barrier to sustainability, dignity, and well-being. The system should not be creating fear for people who are already vulnerable.

Number three, what this petition asks for. My petition asks for a clear, practical change. Number one is remove Support Living Payment reviews for people with medically certified long life disabilities. If a disability is permanent, the income support should be permanent. Number two, create a permanent Support Living Payment category. This would align with MSD and with MASCC as a medical reality. Number three, shift review by default to review only if circumstances change. If income changes, if living situations change, review it, but don't review the

disability itself when it is medically confirmed as lifelong. Number four, reduce administrative flow on MSD. This change frees staff to focus on people whose situations generally require reassessment. This is not a radical change. It is a correction of an outdated process. Number four, why this change is responsible and necessary.

This change is medically sound. Lifelong disabilities do not improve. Cost-effective. Fewer unnecessary reviews. Ethical means reduces harm and stress. Practical aligns MSD and NASC and medical certifications. Dignified respects disabled people as citizens, not cases to be reproven. This is a small administrative shift with a large human impact.

Here is my closing statement. In closing, I want to emphasize one thing. People with lifelong disabilities deserve sustainability, dignity, and freedom from unnecessary bureaucratic stress. Removing these reviews is a simple, compassionate, and effective change that will make real difference in people's lives.

All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Donaldson. And Celia Wade-Brown. Good afternoon, Byron. Thank you for preparing the petition and speaking to us today. I had a question about whether you knew people or had heard of people who are Supported Living Payment recipients who have got something called Simplified Access so that they don't have their capacity to work reassessed.

Not that I'm aware of. Thank you. And you obviously have great experience in your own situation. Do you also network with other people in a similar situation? Well, I'm not really around a lot of people, you see. So I have to say no. That's fine.

Yeah. Your experience is valid, and thank you for bringing it. All right. Well, look, thank you, Byron. Just one question I was going to ask is that with the changes in the type of opportunities available for people, I'm really talking probably more about the changes in technology, that as the opportunities to use technology increase, do you think it's fair to say that it would be as we

do increase that capability, that it's fair to see whether some of the people who are on the Supported Living may be able to participate in a way they couldn't before? Do you understand what I'm saying? Yeah. I think I might know what you are saying.

When you say technology, are you meaning like when they go onto the online portal or something on- Yes... of the MSD website? Yeah. Things like- Something like that... a world that didn't exist probably as recently as 20 years ago, that now the opportunities available for people.

Given that there generally tends to be a belief that the more people are given the opportunity to participate in the workforce, or in whatever capacity they have, do you think that's worth reassessing at different times? Yes. If it seems they are capable of doing so, yes, I do think that is possible.

All right. Well, look, thank you very much. That was just something I wanted to articulate. So thank you very much. Now, you're welcome to remain online. We now have submissions from the Ministry of Social Development, and CCS Disability Action, and the New Zealand Disability Network.

So you're welcome to remain on for that. So first up, we've got the Ministry of Social Development, and I'll let you introduce yourselves in 10 minutes, and hopefully leave time for some questions. Thank you, Chair. My name is Dee Collins. I'm a manager of the Income Support team at the Ministry of Social Development, along with Sam Willis, who signed the written response we provided the committee.

I'm here with Dayna Vertigen. She is an operational policy senior advisor. So we can take some questions at the end of my submission. I won't go on for too long. Our understanding is that Mr. Donaldson is calling for the removal of reviews for Supported Living Payment recipients who have disabilities that have been medically verified as being permanent and lifelong.

I'm briefly going to explain the types of reviews that people on the Supported Living Payment receive. I'm not going to talk about Supported Living Payment on the grounds of caring for someone who might be in need of full-time care. You can get SLP as a carer. I'm focusing on the eligibility and the reviews for people who have the Supported Living Payment on the grounds of health condition, disability, and injury. Eligibility for the Supported Living Payment is underpinned by an assessment of a person's work capacity,

rather than just having a health condition, disability, or injury. This is because a key purpose of the welfare system is to support people to find and remain in employment. A non-reviewable category of the Supported Living Payment already does exist, and that is called the Simplified Access process.

So, to receive the Supported Living Payment, you need to be permanently and severely restricted in your capacity to work due to a health condition and disability. But Simplified Access can be provided to people who have specific diagnoses. That means that their capacity to work is unlikely to ever improve, that they could regularly work 15 hours or more a week in open employment.

Sorry. Do you mind just pulling the microphone a little bit closer? Sure. Hopefully it won't be- Thank you... too close So people can be granted the Support and Living Payment through simplified access as part of the application process, and this information might come from the medical certificate and the doctor's notes in a work capacity medical certificate form, or through a needs assessment that might set out that the person needs support in all aspects of their life.

There are some conditions that we would count automatically towards simplified access, such as total blindness, terminal illness with a life expectancy of 24 months or less, severe intellectual or cognitive impairment, and then a disorder that's reached the stage of deterioration to the extent that the condition severely impacts on a person's ability to function that is unlikely to improve. So generally, that would be that a person requires constant assistance from others for all aspect of their personal care, for things like showering, meal preparation, eating.

At the end of March this year, there were 108,500 people on the Support and Living Payment and on the carer payment, and about 12% of those received access through simplified access. That's about 13,500 people. Sorry, could you say those numbers again slowly, please?

Yeah. Or are they in your- They're on our website. Yeah. So they're- They're not in the- No, I didn't see them No, they're not in the submission, but- So what were those numbers again? There's about 108,498 people receiving the Supported Living Payment in total. So that may include carers, and about 12% and around 13,500 are accessing it on simplified access.

Thank you. That's excellent. You're welcome. So I'm now going to just talk about the two types of reviews you generally would be required to complete as part of the Supported Living Payment. The first is medical reviews, and the second is a review called confirming your circumstances or mandatory reviews. So medical reviews require people who are granted the Supported Living Payment who don't qualify for simplified access to be reassessed every two years to ensure they continue to meet the medical qualifications.

That is, they are both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work. This review is required because a person's work capacity may change over time, and the impact of their health condition on their capacity to work may change over time. It may deteriorate, or it may improve. This is not necessarily because the person's condition has improved or resolved, but it may be because with support, they may be able to engage in some work preparation or employment.

People can provide a new medical certificate for a medical review with their health practitioner, or they may be able to provide another suitable recent assessment as long as the assessment provides the information that MSD can use to determine eligibility. Using information already available from existing assessments is intended to make that review process easier for people.

The second review is a review of circumstances, or also called mandatory reviews, and these are done every 52 weeks. And their purpose is to check that people are receiving the correct rate of assistance and that they continue to be eligible. So this review is generally confirming that the information MSD has about people is correct, and especially those that may impact the rate of assistance and the type of assistance.

So things like income, relationship status, whether they have dependent children in their care. If they're receiving the accommodation supplement or the disability allowance, we'll verify that that hasn't changed or increased or decreased. It's a really important review to ensure that we pay the correct rate of assistance and that people don't incur a lot of debt through overpayment because of a change in circumstance.

And that is done annually. But we do understand that if people get into debt, that creates a lot of distress because MSD must recover any debt or overpaid benefits. So people must respond to that circumstance review. If they don't respond, their benefit can be suspended. That, again, is to prevent debt or paying inappropriately.

These reviews are not the same as a reapplication. Reapplications are for people who are on job seeker support or who are on a temporary benefit who need to reapply to get that assistance. In closing, I just want to recognize that for some people, the experience of applying for and maintaining their income support is very challenging.

We consider that the simplified access policy does help with that and allows MSD under those criteria just to improve the application process for people who have that permanent and severe condition that's never going to change in accordance with the criteria. But annual reviews remain a really important way for us to check in people's circumstances and ensure that we update our information and don't overpay people.

I just want to thank you for the opportunity to respond, and I'm happy to take questions. That's very helpful. Yes. Well, you actually answered one of my questions by saying about the percentage of people who are on simplified access, and I guess the other 87% or thereabouts, would they know about it generally or not? Because Mr.

Donaldson did not appear to- No... when I asked him about it. Yeah. Yeah. They- I'm not saying whether he's eligible or not, but you know. Of course. Yeah. It's certainly something MSD is one of the decisions in our decision process we must consider when we take on a new application. So we will look for that information and consider whether they qualify for simplified access because- No, sorry, that wasn't my question.

My question was, for those that don't qualify- Oh Would they still necessarily know about it? Because it seems like he didn't really know about that process. Yeah. Is that on our website? I am not too sure about that, sorry. But we can look into that and provide something in writing.

We do try to make sure our clients are aware of the assistance that they may be able to receive. If somebody were to not be assessed for simplified access and they disagree with that, they may review that decision with the Medical Appeals Board. However, of course, that relies on them knowing that exists.

Knowing. Hence the question. I will- Yeah. I will check that for you and- Yeah... provide that in writing. Without jumping ahead to our decision, it would be nice if we had something that we would be able to- Yeah... share with the petitioner. Yeah. And thank you. You've already covered the questions. So just so I'm clear, the simplified access is something that is initiated by and large by the assessor, not by the person themselves.

Yes. And the information that their doctor or the other medical practitioner who's putting that information, they may- Right... recognize that. Our guidance does give some shortcuts. So there is a list of typical conditions that we know meet the criteria. Mm-hmm. Yeah. So our staff will be able to recognize some conditions themselves. Right. But they do have a prompt question to decide how often to review, because it will be to initiate that review.

So they will be considering that as part of the initial application process. Yeah. Thank you. And following on from our Chair's point, when new technology becomes available, for example, voice-to-text or those sorts of things, does that trigger any reassessment of people that you thought might not be able to work but now can?

Or might be able to. Yeah. Yes. Yes, that's correct. So that's why we review work capacity every two years, because there may be opportunities with workplace adaptations to enable people to work. Mm-hmm. And disabled people regularly want, and have expressed that they want to work and would like support to work.

So they may not be necessarily in case management and actively reviewed, but MSD does have the power if they consider a work capacity change has happened or they're informed of that, to then re-review the circumstances and the supports available to people, including the review period. Whether, yeah, they can- Mm-hmm... kind of go back and reassess their work capacity if required.
All right. Well, thank you very much. You're welcome to remain. We're now going to hear from CCS. We've got them online, have we? Yes. Mm-hmm.

And we'd try with this committee just to get to the right place and the right recommendation. So it can become interactive sometimes, which is what's useful. Having to remain just in case something does come up, but- In case you have a question, sure. Yeah. Is my video working? We've got, yeah, I hear a voice there.

Is that- Okay. That's a good start... Ms Eden-Mann? There we go. Hang on one second. We've got a voice there, but no camera. We may have to just go on without a video. Apologies. My laptop appears to be having a midweek meltdown. But that's okay. So I am- All right. Well, carry on. We can certainly hear you anyway. So welcome.

Can you see us? Yes. Yes, I can. All right. You've heard our introduction. So- Yes. Yeah... I look forward to hearing from you. So I am Pippa Eden-Mann. I'm the National Policy Analyst for CCS Disability Action. We strongly support this petition. Our central message today is simple: people with lifelong disabilities, impairments, or health conditions should not be required to repeatedly prove a permanent condition is still permanent in order to retain essential income support. The supported living payment exists primarily for people who are unable to work long-term or permanently

because of a disability, impairment, or health condition. The threshold for receiving the support is already high. People don't receive the supported living payment lightly. They've already had to have gone through rigorous medical assessment and a fairly arduous administrative process before being found eligible. Yet even when a person's condition has been confirmed as lifelong or permanent, they can still be required to complete repeated reviews and provide updated medical evidence.

For many disabled people, this is not a neutral administrative step. It can involve cost, stress, uncertainty, and real risk. A person may need to book and pay for a GP appointment simply to confirm what is already known, that their disability or health condition has not disappeared. For disabled people who already experience higher rates of financial hardship, that cost is not minor.

It may mean choosing between medical paperwork and other essential living costs. One in five disabled people cannot afford to go to the GP when they need to. The consequences of not completing a review can also be severe. If a person cannot secure an appointment in time, cannot afford the appointment, misses correspondence, or struggles to navigate the process, their payments may be delayed, suspended, or canceled.

For people who rely on this income to meet basic needs, that risk is significant. It is particularly concerning because the welfare system can be complex and difficult to navigate. Many disabled people do not know about simplified access, and many medical professionals are also unclear about the process and what qualifies as well.

Disabled people should not be placed in a position where the continuation of essential support depends on repeatedly engaging with processes that are not always accessible, user-centered, or proportionate to their circumstances. There's also a wider systems issue. General practice is under significant pressure.

It's not a good use of scarce medical appointments for GPs to repeatedly complete paperwork confirming that permanent conditions that have already been assessed are still permanent. That time could be better directed towards people who are seeking care for acute medical health needs. The same applies to the welfare system.

MSD staff time and public resources shouldn't be spent on reassessing circumstances where the outcome's already known. Repeated medical reviews of lifelong disabilities do not make the system fairer or more effective. They create unnecessary administration and unnecessary harm.

And this practice is also inconsistent with a rights-based approach to disability. It undermines a disabled person's dignity. It tells disabled people that they must continue to justify their existence and their need for support when their disability or condition is permanent. Conditions like Down syndrome, significant lifelong conditions such as autism, or permanent loss of function don't disappear because another two years has passed. We acknowledge that public systems do require accountability.

However, accountability should be targeted, proportionate, and evidence-based. It should not impose recurring burdens on people whose eligibility rests on the conditions already confirmed as permanent and irreversible. For these reasons, CCS Disability Action recommends that the government end the periodic medical reviews for supported living payment recipients with medically confirmed permanent disabilities, impairments, or health conditions that will not improve over time. We also recommend working with disabled people,

disability organizations, and medical professionals to develop clear and consistent criteria for conditions, disabilities, and impairments that should be treated as permanent and irreversible for the purpose of review exemptions such as the simplified access. In addition, we are also recommending wider consultation with the disability community about how to reduce barriers within the welfare system and ensure that the processes are accessible and user-centered and consistent with the dignity and rights of disabled people. Disabled people with lifelong disabilities should not have to

repeatedly prove that they are still disabled in order to receive the support that they need to live. The current review requirements cause avoidable stress, impose avoidable costs, and use public resources in ways that don't serve disabled people, medical professionals, or the welfare system well.

Permanent disability should be recognized as permanent. CCS Disability Action therefore supports the petition and urges the government to remove supported living payment medical benefit reviews for people with lifelong and permanent disabilities. And I'm happy to take any questions. Yeah, just one question. In this, do you differentiate at all between those with intellectual disabilities versus physical disabilities?

It depends, but likely no, because some permanent disability, like some permanent physical disabilities, you're still unable to work permanently. You don't necessarily have to have a permanent intellectual or neurological condition for it to permanently affect your ability to work over the course of your life.

All right. Thank you. Selina Brown. Yes. I think we can all agree that there are some impairments that will improve and some that won't. And I guess the question is whether we've got... And some that improve, that's fine. Two years on, they'll be able to work.

But it seems to me that 12% of the total supported living payments, would you think that's quite small? Do you have any- Yes... statistics as to how many- No. Hang on, Debbie, let's finish the question. Any statistics, out of that 108 and half thousand people who are on the supported living payment, do you have any estimates or evidence as to what percentage you think would have permanent disabilities?

I can't give you a number off the top of my head, but in my nearly decade of experience in the disability sector and as a disabled person myself, it would be higher than 12%. And I can also tell you that navigating the process to access SLP and to even know about the things like simplified access, people don't know about simplified access.

Medical professionals are even unclear. So you might be signed off as having a permanent condition that permanently affects your ability to work over the course of your life 15 hours a week or less, but there's a lot of confusion and not a lot of clarity about what to do with the people who have conditions that aren't specifically listed by MSD, but still should be falling under the simplified access category.

And do you know anywhere where that data as the percentage of people on SLP who, if the system was simpler, you think might qualify for simplified assessments? The state of disability data in New Zealand is fairly poor. It has a lot to do with the way that we collect disability data.

We use a question set called the Washington Group Short Set, which undercounts disabled people, so it all gets a bit muddly. But I would guess that there would need to be research into that from MSD's end, because they're the ones in charge of this money.

Yes. All right. Look, well, thank you very much. You're welcome to remain on the line. We're now just going to hear from New Zealand Disability Support Network. We have Ms. Hughes here. She coming through now. Is that coming in now, did you say?
Yeah.

That's just in. Ah. Yes, good afternoon, Ms. Hughes. Have you been listening to the submissions today? Indeed, I have. Yes. Great to be here. Thank you. All right. You're welcome, and we'll love to hear from you, and we've got 10 minutes. Lovely. Thank you so much. Kia ora koutou.

Ko Debbie Hughes toku ingoa. I am the Chief Executive of the New Zealand Disability Support Network, or NZDSN. NZDSN is the national peak body representing disability support providers across Aotearoa. Our members support disabled people to live good lives, participate in their communities, and where possible, access meaningful employment.

Thank you for the opportunity to speak to our submission on Byron Donaldson's petition concerning supported living payment reassessments for people with lifelong disabilities. I want to begin by acknowledging the concern at the heart of this petition. No disabled person should be repeatedly required to prove that they still have a permanent disability or medical condition that will not change. This can be stressful and demeaning for disabled people and their families, as well as creating unnecessary administrative work.

Importantly, MSD already has a process to address this. Through its simplified access process, MSD can identify people whose condition is permanent and whose circumstances mean they should not be required to repeatedly provide medical evidence or undergo assessment. We support that existing approach.

Where it is clear that a person's circumstances will not change, they should continue to be exempt from repeated reassessment. Our concern is therefore not with protecting people from unnecessary reassessment. We agree with that. Our concern is with using the broader category of lifelong disability as the basis for automatically exempting everyone from any future review or discussion about employment.

There is an important difference between having a lifelong disability and having no current or future capacity to participate in employment. Those are not the same thing. Mm-hmm. A disability may be lifelong, but its impact on a person's life and the opportunities available to that person can change considerably over time.

People gain skills. They complete education and training. Their health or personal circumstances change. New technology becomes available. Workplaces become more accessible. Employers become more flexible. More importantly, people may gain access to the right support at the right time.

A diagnosis alone cannot tell us whether someone can work. Autism, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, intellectual disability, blindness, and deafness are all lifelong disabilities. But the impact on each of these disabilities varies significantly from person to person.

Many people with lifelong disabilities are already participating successfully in the workforce- Mm-hmm... sometimes independently and sometimes with ongoing support or workplace accommodations. If we automatically exempted everyone with a lifelong disability from any future consideration of employment, we would risk making a very different and equally damaging assumption that lifelong disability means lifelong incapacity.

Mm. That is not consistent with the New Zealand Disability Strategy, Enabling Good Lives, or the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Article 27 of the convention affirms the right of disabled people to work on an equal basis with others. That requires us to create genuine pathways into employment and provide the support and reasonable accommodation people need to succeed.

Employment is not the right outcome for every person, and paid work should never be treated as the measure of a person's value. Disabled people contribute to their families and communities in many different ways. However, when employment is possible and wanted, it can bring greater financial independence, stronger social connection, increased confidence, and a sense of purpose and greater choice and control.

We should be careful not to design a system that unintentionally closes that door. Our concern is that a blanket exemption based solely on a lifelong diagnosis could result in people being written off too early and potentially for the rest of their lives. However, retaining periodic reviews is only useful if those reviews are fair, humane, and genuinely supportive.

A review should not simply require a disabled people to repeatedly prove their eligibility for income support. It should not begin from a position of suspicion or create fear that essential financial support will be removed. At its best, a review should be a constructive checkpoint. It should consider whether the person's circumstances or aspirations have changed, and whether new services, training, technology, or workplace support could help them pursue employment if that is what they want.

If we continue to review people but do not provide meaningful pathways into employment, we have retained the burden, but without delivering the benefit. There is little value in repeatedly asking whether a person can work if suitable employment services are unavailable, workplaces remain inaccessible, or employers are unwilling to provide reasonable accommodation.

The quality and purpose of the review process therefore matter just as much as its frequency. NZDSN's position is that MSD should retain its existing simplified access process for people who should not be subjected to repeated reassessment.

For other people with lifelong disabilities, some form of proportionate periodic review may remain appropriate. That review should be individualized and consider the functional impact of the person's disability, their circumstances, their aspirations, and the support available to them.

It should not rely on diagnosis alone, and it should not assume that eligibility for income support disappears simply because a person may be able to undertake some work. This is not a choice between protecting disabled people from unnecessary reassessment and supporting disabled people into employment. We can and should do both.

We therefore recommend that the existing exemption process remains available to people whose circumstances clearly warrant it. We also recommend retaining proportionate periodic reviews for others where there may be potential or a desire to participate in employment now or in the future.

These decisions should be based on the individual and the functional impact of their disability, not simply whether their diagnosis is lifelong. Finally, any employment-focused review must be connected to real and adequately resourced support. A review should open doors. It should not simply test eligibility or threaten a person's financial security.

We support the intent of the petition to protect disabled people from unnecessary stress and indignity. However, in seeking to remove one barrier, we must not create another by institutionalizing low expectations and permanently excluding people from opportunities they may want to and be able to pursue in the future.

The existing simplified access process should protect people for whom a reassessment serves no purpose. For others, the system should continue to recognize their potential, respond to their aspirations, and provide the support that makes participation possible. That is the balance we are asking the committee to maintain.

Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions. All right. Thank you very much. Members, questions? Thank you. And that's very insightful. As a parent of a high and complex disabled child, I think we all hope that at some stage they may be able to participate in the workforce in some manner.

So, if I can say that. So look, thank you very much, and thank you to all our submitters, including Mr. Donaldson, who I hope you're still there. Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We'll be reporting this back to the House once the committee has discussed and agreed with what our recommendation should be. So thank you very much, everyone.
Lovely. Thank you so much. All right.
